To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

C-terminal PTHrP fragments 107–138 and 107–111 were without significant inhibitory effects on isolated rat and chicken osteoclasts, and the lack of significant effect was not due to the absence of a PTHrP receptor.
C-terminal fragments of parathyroid hormone related protein (PTHr) were without effect on resorptive activity in isolated osteoclast assays.
PTHrP fragments 107–139, 107–111 and 107–138 are not inhibitory on isolated rat and chicken osteoclasts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of carboxyl terminal fragments of PTH-related protein (107–111,107–138 and107–139) on the resorbing activity of isolated chick and rat osteoclasts in vitro.
the effect of PTHrPs on isolated osteoclast activity and bone resorption.
determining the effects of carboxyl terminal fragments of parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP), on isolated osteoclast activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the C-terminal fragments of human parathyroid hormone–related protein (hPTHrP) do not significantly alter the resorption of isolated rat and/or chick osteoclast preparations in a dose-dependent manner over the concentration range 10-9 M-10-13 M.
the PTHrP fragments tested in this study do not appear to have a significant inhibitory effect at the osteoclast level.
PTHrP fragments 107–138 and 107–111 have no consistent effect on isolated osteoclast resorptive activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the absence of calcitonin, these PTHrP fragments have no significant effect on isolated rat and chicken osteoclasts, and that calcitonin is the only known potent inhibitor of isolated osteoclastic activity.
, in the rat and chicken, the C-terminal PTHrP peptides 107–111 (PTHrP 107–111), 107–138 (PTHrP107–138), and 107–39 (PTHrP(107–139)) are without significant effects on isolated osteoclast activity.
, although the C-terminal PTHrP fragments 107–138 and 107–111 do have some biological activity, they are not potent inhibitors of osteoclastic activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the osteoclast is not the primary target for PTHrP fragments in vivo, but rather, the osteoblast.
PTHrP fragments 107–139 and 107–111 have no effect on the resorption of isolated osteoclastic cells.
PTHrP fragments do not have a consistent effect on isolated osteoclast activity, and thus, the effect of these fragments on osteoclasts in vivo may be different than that observed in vitro.
